beef-and-noodles-with-mushroom-sauce.title: Beef and noodles with mushroom sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Beef and noodles with mushroom sauce is a hearty dish that combines tender pieces of beef, al dente noodles, and a flavorful sauce made from mushrooms, cream, and spices. The dish is popular in both European and Asian cuisines, easy to prepare at home, and suitable for lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef is one of the richest sources of iron and vitamin B12.
Mushrooms contain vitamin D, which is rare in plant foods.
Traditionally, the noodles used in such dishes were egg‑based, giving them a golden color and firm texture.
Mushroom sauce is often enriched with cream to mellow the natural earthiness of the mushrooms.
The recipe can be adapted for a gluten‑free diet by substituting wheat noodles with rice or buckwheat noodles.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Cream supplies calcium while beef adds iron, both important for bone health and blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: The dish delivers vitamins B6 and B12, crucial for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from mushrooms
items.content: Mushrooms contain selenium and polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy replenishment
items.content: Carbohydrates from the noodles quickly restore glycogen stores, providing energy after physical activity.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Beef and cream can raise cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: The sauce is often seasoned with salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Mushroom allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Beef must be cooked thoroughly to avoid salmonella and other bacterial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, garnished with fresh herbs such as parsley or dill. A sprinkle of grated Parmesan or a dash of hot sauce can be added to taste. It pairs well with a light mixed‑green salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. When reheating, add a splash of cream or broth to keep the sauce from drying out. If freezing, omit the noodles, as they can become mushy.

content.title: About
content.content: Duck is a waterfowl bird whose meat is prized for its rich flavor and tender texture. Cooked duck without skin contains less fat than with skin while still providing a high amount of protein, B‑vitamins, and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Domesticated duck dates back over 4,000 years in China and Egypt.
Duck meat is a good source of iron, helping to prevent anemia.
In many cuisines (e.g., French, Chinese) duck is often served with fruit‑based sauces.
Ducks migrate long distances, which can affect the composition of their meat depending on the season.
Most of the fat in duck is in the skin, which is why it is frequently removed to lower calorie content.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Duck meat provides about 19 g of protein per 100 g, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12, niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), which aid nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals: iron and zinc
items.content: Iron helps transport oxygen, while zinc supports immune responses.

items.title: Low carbohydrate content
items.content: Duck contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Polyunsaturated fatty acids
items.content: Even without skin, the meat retains beneficial omega‑3 and omega‑6 fatty acids.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bird meat.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Duck, even skinless, contains moderate cholesterol; people with hypercholesterolemia should monitor portions.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Despite skin removal, duck remains calorie‑dense due to intramuscular fat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skinless duck can be roasted, braised, grilled, or oven‑baked. Remove the skin and excess fat before seasoning with salt, pepper, and herbs. Serve with vegetables, fruit sauces, or whole‑grain sides.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh duck refrigerated at 0–4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw frozen duck in the refrigerator before cooking.

egg-sandwich-on-wheat-bread-with-cheese.title: Egg sandwich on wheat bread, with cheese

content.title: About
content.content: An egg sandwich on wheat bread with cheese is a simple, nutritious snack made of a boiled or fried egg, melted or sliced cheese, and two slices of whole‑grain wheat bread. The combination of protein, healthy fats, and complex carbohydrates makes it a convenient option for breakfast or a light lunch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat bread provides slow‑release energy thanks to its fiber content.
Eggs are one of the most affordable complete protein sources, containing all essential amino acids.
Cheese adds calcium and vitamin D, supporting bone health.
The sandwich is easily customizable – add vegetables, herbs, or spices to taste.
Different countries have their own twists: in the US bacon is common, while in Japan mayo and soy sauce are popular additions.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: A single egg provides about 6 g of high‑quality protein, helping maintain muscle mass and satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamins B2, B6, and B12, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese contributes a notable amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Whole‑grain wheat bread supplies fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: Small amounts of monounsaturated fats from cheese and egg support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs or cheese, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese often contains a lot of salt; people monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt or reduced‑fat varieties.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich can be calorie‑dense, especially when using full‑fat cheese; portion control is advisable.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; those with elevated cholesterol levels should consume them in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sandwich hot, lightly toasting the bread until golden, or cold. Add lettuce, tomato, or avocado for extra nutrients and flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: A prepared sandwich can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours in an airtight container. For longer storage, keep the components separate and assemble just before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen yogurt is a frozen dessert made from yogurt, offering a smoother texture than ice cream and a mildly tangy flavor. It typically contains yogurt, milk, sugar, and live probiotic cultures, making it a healthier alternative to traditional ice cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frozen yogurt originated in the United States in the 1970s as a healthier ice cream alternative.
It is often served with a variety of toppings such as fruit, nuts, chocolate, and granola.
The probiotics in yogurt can support gut health.
Compared to regular ice cream, frozen yogurt usually has less fat.
Texture can range from creamy to airy depending on the amount of air incorporated (overrun).

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: Live cultures help maintain a balanced gut microbiome and support the immune system.

items.title: Source of calcium and protein
items.content: Yogurt provides calcium for bones and protein for tissue repair.

items.title: Lower fat content
items.content: Frozen yogurt typically contains less saturated fat than traditional ice cream.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yogurt supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: May reduce overeating
items.content: The tangy taste can promote quicker satiety.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some varieties contain added sugar, increasing calorie count.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to dairy may react to frozen yogurt.

items.title: Probiotics and immune status
items.content: Those with compromised immune systems should consult a doctor before consuming live cultures.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve frozen yogurt in cones or cups, add fresh berries, fruit, nuts, honey, or chocolate sauce. It can also be used as a base for smoothies or dessert parfaits.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen yogurt in the freezer at –18 °C. After opening, consume within 1–2 days to maintain texture and probiotic activity.

content.title: About
content.content: Capri Sun is a ready‑to‑drink fruit juice beverage packaged in convenient pouches. It is made from concentrated fruit juices, water, sugar and a small amount of vitamins. The drink is popular with children and adults alike because of its bright taste and practical packaging.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first Capri Sun product was launched in 1977 in Germany.
The pouch is made of multi‑layer material that does not require a cap – you simply tear off a corner.
The range includes more than 30 flavors, such as apple, orange, tropical mix and berry blends.
Capri Sun is often used in school lunchboxes thanks to its easy transport and lack of glass.
In some countries the drink is sold without added sugar, using only sweeteners.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: The fruit juices provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The beverage contains about 90 % water, helping to maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Sugar and fruit carbohydrates supply quick energy, useful during active play or exercise.

items.title: Electrolytes
items.content: Some flavors include small amounts of sodium and potassium, aiding electrolyte replenishment.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Regular versions can contain up to 10 g of sugar per 100 ml, which may contribute to tooth decay and weight gain if consumed excessively.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Certain flavors may contain traces of nuts, soy or dairy, which is important for people with allergies.

items.title: Plastic packaging
items.content: Single‑use pouches create environmental waste; proper disposal is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tear open the corner of the pouch and pour the drink into a glass or bottle. You can add ice or dilute with water to taste. The beverage is convenient for school, outings or the gym.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened pouches in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, it is best to consume within 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Lime is a small citrus fruit with green skin and very sour, aromatic flesh. There are varieties such as key lime and Persian lime. Lime is squeezed into drinks, sauces, marinades, and dressings and used in desserts, and its zest is added for aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: British sailors were once supplied with lime juice to prevent scurvy, which is where the nickname limey came from.
Lime is used in margarita and mojito cocktails and in Latin American and Asian dishes.
In ceviche, lime juice cooks raw fish through its acidity.
Unripe limes are green, while fully ripe ones turn yellow.
The acidity and zest of lime pair well with fish, meat, and vegetables.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains flavonoids
items.content: Citrus flavonoids have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Lime juice adds almost no calories.

items.title: Adds flavor without salt
items.content: The acidity and aroma of lime make it possible to use less salt in dishes.

items.title: Refreshing
items.content: Lime makes drinks and dishes fresher and brighter.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Lime is very acidic and may cause heartburn and damage tooth enamel.

items.title: Sunburns
items.content: Lime juice on the skin together with sunlight can cause phytophotodermatitis, with burns and dark marks; wash the skin after contact.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Citrus fruits can cause allergic reactions.

items.title: Zest
items.content: Wash the fruit thoroughly before using the zest.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Squeeze lime into drinks, sauces, dressings, marinades, soups, and desserts. Roll it on the counter before squeezing to get more juice. Grate the zest into baked goods and dishes. Serve lime with fish, meat, tacos, and vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole limes at room temperature for about a week or in the refrigerator for two to four weeks. Keep squeezed juice in the refrigerator for a few days or freeze it in ice cube trays. The zest can be frozen.

content.title: About
content.content: Mayonnaise is an emulsion of vegetable oil, eggs, vinegar or lemon juice, and seasonings. Regular mayonnaise has a creamy texture, a slightly tangy taste, and is used as a dressing, sauce, and culinary ingredient.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recorded recipe appeared in 1756 in France and was named after the town of Mahon.
Traditional mayonnaise is made with egg yolk, which acts as an emulsifier linking water and oil.
Different countries have their own twists: in Russia mustard is often added, in Japan rice vinegar is common.
Mayonnaise can be kept in the refrigerator for 2–3 months after opening if stored properly.
There are “light” versions with reduced fat, where part of the oil is replaced by water or yogurt.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: High fat content provides a quick source of calories, useful for increased energy needs.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs supply vitamin B12, riboflavin, and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Mayonnaise helps absorb fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) from other foods in a dish.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Excessive consumption may contribute to weight gain and elevated cholesterol levels.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Mayonnaise contains eggs and can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Bacterial risk if not stored properly
items.content: At temperatures above 4 °C, eggs can become a source of salmonella; keep mayonnaise refrigerated.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Mayonnaise is suitable for salad dressings, sandwich spreads, sauces (e.g., tartar), marinades, and as a base for dips. It can be thinned with milk or yogurt for a lighter texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store mayonnaise in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C in its original container. After opening, use within 2–3 months. Do not leave the opened product at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato home fries (NFS) are diced or sliced tubers fried until golden and crispy. The product is ready to eat after reheating and is commonly used as a side dish or snack in fast‑food outlets and cafeterias.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato is the fourth most produced crop worldwide after rice, wheat and corn.
The term “home fries” originated in the United States in the early 20th century to describe pan‑fried potatoes without breading.
NFS (Not From Scratch) indicates the product is ready‑to‑use without further preparation.
Properly packaged potato slices can retain a crunchy texture for up to 12 months.
In the US home fries are often served with sour cream and chives.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C source
items.content: Vitamin C helps boost immunity and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs give sustained energy and help maintain stable blood glucose levels.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Skin and small amounts of fiber aid digestive health.

items.title: Beta‑carotene
items.content: Yellow and orange varieties contain beta‑carotene, a precursor of vitamin A important for vision.

items.title: High carbohydrate content
items.content: Large portions can raise blood sugar, which is relevant for people with diabetes.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Overheating can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen; fry at ≤180 °C.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Rare but possible allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Salt and fat
items.content: The product is often salted and fried in oil, increasing sodium and calorie content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reheat in a microwave or skillet until golden. Serve as a side with meat, fish, or as a snack with sauces, sour cream or ketchup.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in a cool, dry place at 0 °C–4 °C. Shelf life is up to 12 months. Discard if a rancid smell or discoloration appears.

rice-brown-cooked-fat-added-made-with-oi.title: Brown Rice, Cooked, Fat Added, Made with Oil

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain rice that retains its bran layer and germ. When cooked with added fat (oil) it becomes more aromatic, more nutrient‑dense, and easier to digest.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice provides more fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals than white rice.
Cooking rice with oil enhances flavor and aids absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
There are over 40 varieties of brown rice worldwide, each with a distinct aroma and texture.
Brown rice is a staple in Asian cuisines, used in pilafs, fried rice, and salads.
When stored in a cool, dry place, whole grains can stay fresh for up to a year.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of magnesium and selenium
items.content: These minerals aid muscle function, nervous system health, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Contains vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E from the added oil protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Heart‑healthy
items.content: The combination of whole grains and healthy fats can help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: May reduce type 2 diabetes risk
items.content: Brown rice’s low glycemic index helps maintain stable post‑meal glucose levels.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Adding oil increases the energy content of a serving, so portion control is important.

items.title: Arsenic content
items.content: Like many whole grains, brown rice can contain trace amounts of arsenic; varied diets are recommended.

items.title: Oil allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to certain plant oils should avoid this preparation.

items.title: Digestive sensitivity
items.content: High fiber may cause bloating or discomfort in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice as a side dish with vegetables, meat, or fish. It works well in salads, soups, casseroles, or as a base for vegetarian bowls. Feel free to season with herbs, spices, or soy sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice should be refrigerated and eaten within 3‑4 days, or frozen in a sealed container for longer storage.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice, fried, meatless is a ready‑to‑eat dish made from cooked rice stir‑fried with vegetables and spices. It contains no meat, making it suitable for vegetarians and those limiting animal protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fried rice originated in Asian cuisines as a way to use leftover cooked rice.
Meatless versions often include soy chunks or tofu to boost protein content.
Typical vegetables are carrots, peas, corn, bell pepper and green onions, giving the dish color and nutrients.
Flavor is commonly enhanced with soy sauce, ginger, garlic and sesame oil.
It can be reheated in a microwave or skillet in 2‑3 minutes.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides sustained energy through slow‑release glucose.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Meatless versions are usually cooked with a small amount of oil, fitting low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains thiamine, niacin and vitamin B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains plant protein
items.content: Soy or tofu additions increase protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables add fiber, aiding healthy digestion.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: If soy chunks are used, people with soy allergy should avoid the product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce can raise salt levels; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Gluten in sauces
items.content: Some sauces may contain gluten; select gluten‑free options for celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready after reheating. Serve it as a main dish, add to salads, use in wraps, or as a side to vegetable patties.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in the original package for up to 5 days after opening. Freeze for up to 3 months. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Sausage with tomato-based sauce is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of boiled or smoked meat sausage covered with a thick tomato‑based sauce seasoned with herbs and spices. It is commonly sold in portion‑size cans or pouches and is intended for quick heating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tomato sauce gives the sausage a characteristic sweet‑sour flavor and a bright red color.
These combinations are traditional in Eastern European cuisines, where they are popular as a fast‑lunch dish.
The meat‑tomato blend increases lycopene content, a powerful antioxidant.
The product is widely used in school cafeterias and camping meals because of its long shelf life.
Some recipes add paprika or chili for a mild heat.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The sausage provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Meat in the product contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Lycopene from tomatoes
items.content: Tomato sauce supplies lycopene, supporting heart health and offering anti‑inflammatory effects.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Convenient and time‑saving
items.content: A ready‑made meal allows a quick, satisfying dinner without additional cooking steps.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sausage products often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure if consumed frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Meat sausages may be high in saturated fats, which should be limited in cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to sausage ingredients.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: To extend shelf life, nitrites and other preservatives may be used, which some people prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the product in a microwave or on the stove until the sauce bubbles, then serve hot. It can be mixed with pasta, rice, mashed potatoes, or used as a sandwich filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened package in a cool, dry place. After opening, store in the refrigerator and consume within 3‑4 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Sushi with tuna is a traditional Japanese dish consisting of bite‑size rolls of vinegared rice topped with fresh tuna and wrapped in a sheet of nori. The tuna gives the sushi a rich flavor and a boost of omega‑3 fatty acids.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna is one of the most prized fish in Japan and is a staple in sushi restaurants.
Sushi originated in Southeast Asia as a method of preserving fish and evolved into an art form in Japan.
It is traditionally served with soy sauce, wasabi, and pickled ginger.
Several species of tuna are used for sushi: yellowfin (ahi), bigeye, and albacore.
In Japan, a “sushi‑meister” is a master chef who has completed years of apprenticeship.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Tuna provides EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Sushi with tuna delivers complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One roll typically contains about 40‑50 kcal, making it a weight‑friendly option.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tuna is a good source of vitamin B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish provides selenium, magnesium, and iron, which support immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Parasite risk
items.content: Raw fish can harbor parasites; only use sushi‑grade tuna.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Tuna can accumulate mercury; pregnant women and children should limit intake.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood.

items.title: Sodium in soy sauce
items.content: Excessive soy sauce adds a lot of sodium to the meal.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sushi with tuna is typically eaten with fingers or chopsticks, dipped lightly in soy sauce with a dab of wasabi. Pickled ginger can be consumed between pieces to cleanse the palate.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared sushi in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours in an airtight container. For longer storage, freeze the fish and keep the rice chilled to prevent spoilage.

teriyaki-chicken-with-rice-and-vegetable.title: Teriyaki Chicken with Rice and Vegetables (Diet Frozen Meal)

content.title: About
content.content: Teriyaki chicken with rice and vegetables is a ready‑to‑heat frozen meal designed for diet‑friendly nutrition. It features tender chicken breast glazed with a sweet‑savory teriyaki sauce, served over steamed rice and a mix of vegetables (broccoli, carrots, peas). The meal provides approximately 350 kcal, 30 g of protein and minimal fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Teriyaki sauce originates from Japan and is traditionally made from soy sauce, mirin, sugar and ginger.
Chicken used in frozen meals is often pre‑marinated, which helps retain juiciness after heating.
The rice is typically long‑grain basmati, offering a lower glycemic index compared with short‑grain varieties.
Vegetables are flash‑frozen at peak freshness, preserving most of their vitamins and minerals.
The meal can be stored in the freezer for up to 12 months without quality loss.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Chicken breast supplies about 30 g of complete protein, essential for maintaining muscle mass.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: The dish contains less than 5 g of fat, mostly polyunsaturated, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Soy sauce and chicken provide B6 and B12 vitamins, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: The vegetables and rice contribute fiber that aids regular digestion.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: At roughly 350 kcal per serving, it fits well into weight‑management plans.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Soy sauce may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Teriyaki sauce contains a noticeable amount of salt; people monitoring sodium intake should account for it.

items.title: Requires thorough heating
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave live bacteria; heat to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Not suitable for children under 3
items.content: The firm texture of rice and vegetable pieces can pose a choking hazard for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Microwave or steam the meal until fully hot (about 5‑7 minutes), ensuring the center reaches 75 °C. Serve immediately; optionally garnish with fresh lemon juice or chopped green onions for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C or lower. Once the package is opened, store the remaining portion in an airtight container in the refrigerator and consume within 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Meat-filled tortellini are small ring‑shaped pasta made from egg dough and a meat filling (beef, pork, or a blend). They are served without sauce, allowing the flavor of the filling and the texture of the dough to shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tortellini originate from Italy and their shape resembles tiny ears.
Traditionally they are hand‑rolled, but modern production often uses automated machines.
The meat filling may be seasoned with nutmeg, Parmesan, and other herbs for extra flavor.
Although often served in broth, serving them plain highlights their delicate structure.
Italy hosts a "Tortellini Festival" celebrating this iconic pasta.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat filling provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Tortellini deliver B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat dough offers slowly digestible carbs that help maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Provides zinc
items.content: Zinc from the meat supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared tortellini may contain added salt; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat dough contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in individuals with celiac disease.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Meat fillings, especially pork, can be high in saturated fat; moderation is advised.

items.title: Food‑borne bacteria risk
items.content: Tortellini should be cooked to an internal temperature of 75 °C to eliminate pathogens.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the plain tortellini in a light broth, drizzle with olive oil and fresh herbs, or simply sprinkle with grated Parmesan. They are eaten with a fork, taking small bites.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry tortellini in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 12 months. Cooked tortellini should be refrigerated in a sealed container for 2–3 days.
